claim: Ascending signals from the thalamus to the sensory neocortex preserve spatially organized information based on layer specificity.
source: Previous studies based on layer specificity suggest that ascending signals from the thalamus to the sensory neocortex preserve spatially organized information, but it remains unknown whether sensory information descending from sensory neocortex to the thalamus also maintains such spatial organization pattern.
evidence: The claim is supported by references to previous studies, indicating citation-based evidence.

claim: It remains unknown whether sensory information descending from sensory neocortex to the thalamus maintains spatial organization pattern.
source: Previous studies based on layer specificity suggest that ascending signals from the thalamus to the sensory neocortex preserve spatially organized information, but it remains unknown whether sensory information descending from sensory neocortex to the thalamus also maintains such spatial organization pattern.
evidence: The claim explicitly states a gap in current knowledge.

claim: A clear tonotopic gradient was observed among TR neurons.
source: A clear tonotopic gradient was observed among TR neurons, but not CT neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: No tonotopic gradient was observed among CT neurons.
source: A clear tonotopic gradient was observed among TR neurons, but not CT neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CT neurons exhibited markedly higher heterogeneity in their frequency tuning than TR neurons.
source: Additionally, CT neurons exhibited markedly higher heterogeneity in their frequency tuning and had broader bandwidth than TR neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: CT neurons had broader bandwidth than TR neurons.
source: Additionally, CT neurons exhibited markedly higher heterogeneity in their frequency tuning and had broader bandwidth than TR neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Tonotopic organization is a spatially ordered gradient of neuronal frequency preference in the mammalian auditory system.
source: In the mammalian auditory system, one of the most prominent features is the tonotopic organization – a spatially ordered gradient of neuronal frequency preference (Bizley et al., 2005; Kajikawa et al., 2005; Merzenich et al., 1976; Morel et al., 1993; Nelken et al., 2004; Reale and Imig, 1980; Stiebler et al., 1997; Tani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Clear tonotopic maps have been found in the auditory cortex of humans.
source: Clear tonotopic maps have been found in the auditory cortex (AuC) of many mammalian species, including humans (Clopton et al., 1974; Humphries et al., 2010), macaque monkeys (Hackett and Stepniewska, 1998), cats (Lee et al., 2004), ferrets (Bizley et al., 2005), Mongolian gerbils (Budinger et al., 2000; Ohga et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 1993), rats (Polley et al., 2007), and mice (Guo et al., 2012; King et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Clear tonotopic maps have been found in the auditory cortex of macaque monkeys.
source: Clear tonotopic maps have been found in the auditory cortex (AuC) of many mammalian species, including humans (Clopton et al., 1974; Humphries et al., 2010), macaque monkeys (Hackett and Stepniewska, 1998), cats (Lee et al., 2004), ferrets (Bizley et al., 2005), Mongolian gerbils (Budinger et al., 2000; Ohga et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 1993), rats (Polley et al., 2007), and mice (Guo et al., 2012; King et al., 2018).

source: Clear tonotopic maps have been found in the auditory cortex (AuC) of many mammalian species, including humans (Clopton et al., 1974; Humphries et al., 2010), macaque monkeys (Hackett and Stepniewska, 1998), cats (Lee et al., 2004), ferrets (Bizley et al., 2005), Mongolian gerbils (Budinger et al., 2000; Ohga et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 1993), rats (Polley et al., 2007), and mice (Guo et al., 2012; King et al., 2018).

source: Clear tonotopic maps have been found in the auditory cortex (AuC) of many mammalian species, including humans (Clopton et al., 1974; Humphries et al., 2010), macaque monkeys (Hackett and Stepniewska, 1998), cats (Lee et al., 2004), ferrets (Bizley et al., 2005), Mongolian gerbils (Budinger et al., 2000; Ohga et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 1993), rats (Polley et al., 2007), and mice (Guo et al., 2012; King et al., 2018).

source: Clear tonotopic maps have been found in the auditory cortex (AuC) of many mammalian species, including humans (Clopton et al., 1974; Humphries et al., 2010), macaque monkeys (Hackett and Stepniewska, 1998), cats (Lee et al., 2004), ferrets (Bizley et al., 2005), Mongolian gerbils (Budinger et al., 2000; Ohga et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 1993), rats (Polley et al., 2007), and mice (Guo et al., 2012; King et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tonotopy originates in the cochlea and is relayed and preserved throughout all the ascending stages, including the medial geniculate body (MGB) and the AuC.
source: Tonotopy originates in the cochlea and is relayed and preserved throughout all the ascending stages, including the medial geniculate body (MGB) and the AuC (Jasmin et al., 2019; Simon et al., 2009; Smith and Wever, 1949).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The connections between MGB and AuC play an essential role in the perception of auditory information.
source: As one of the most explored pathways in the auditory system, the connections between MGB and AuC play an essential role in the perception of auditory information (Lee, 2013; Ohga et al., 2017; Pardi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Core fields of the AuC receive their predominant thalamic input from the ventral division of the MGB (MGBv).
source: Core fields of the AuC receive their predominant thalamic input from the ventral division of the MGB (MGBv), which confers well-defined frequency tuning arranged into smoothly varying tonotopic gradients (Andersen et al., 1980; Merzenich and Brugge, 1973; Winer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MGBv confers well-defined frequency tuning arranged into smoothly varying tonotopic gradients.
source: Core fields of the AuC receive their predominant thalamic input from the ventral division of the MGB (MGBv), which confers well-defined frequency tuning arranged into smoothly varying tonotopic gradients (Andersen et al., 1980; Merzenich and Brugge, 1973; Winer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Non-core AuC fields are innervated by non-primary divisions of the MGB and from intracortical inputs originating outside of the AuC.
source: Non-core AuC fields are innervated by non-primary divisions of the MGB and from intracortical inputs originating outside of the AuC (Jones, 2001; Lee and Winer, 2005; Reale and Imig, 1980), which show weak tonotopy and selectivity for processing conspecific communication sounds (Norman-Haignere et al., 2015; Schneider and Woolley, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Non-core AuC fields show weak tonotopy and selectivity for processing conspecific communication sounds.
source: Non-core AuC fields are innervated by non-primary divisions of the MGB and from intracortical inputs originating outside of the AuC (Jones, 2001; Lee and Winer, 2005; Reale and Imig, 1980), which show weak tonotopy and selectivity for processing conspecific communication sounds (Norman-Haignere et al., 2015; Schneider and Woolley, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Feedforward auditory information is conveyed from the MGBv to the AuC, primarily received in layer 4 (L4) but also extending to other layers.
source: Feedforward auditory information is conveyed from the MGBv to the AuC, primarily received in layer 4 (L4) but also extending to other layers (Constantinople and Bruno, 2013; Petreanu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Auditory information is projected corticofugally to downstream targets from either layer 5 (L5) or layer 6 (L6) of the AuC.
source: Subsequently, it is projected corticofugally to downstream targets from either layer 5 (L5) or layer 6 (L6) of the AuC (Shepherd and Yamawaki, 2021), including feedback information to MGB (Happel et al., 2014; Happel et al., 2010; Homma and Bajo, 2021; Kirchgessner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Corticofugal projections from AuC include feedback information to MGB.
source: Subsequently, it is projected corticofugally to downstream targets from either layer 5 (L5) or layer 6 (L6) of the AuC (Shepherd and Yamawaki, 2021), including feedback information to MGB (Happel et al., 2014; Happel et al., 2010; Homma and Bajo, 2021; Kirchgessner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Several studies have revealed the sophisticated inputs and the ability to perceive complex sounds of CT neurons in A1.
source: Several studies have revealed the sophisticated inputs and the ability to perceive complex sounds of CT neurons in A1 (Clayton et al., 2021; Homma et al., 2017), suggesting the descending information flow in the core fields of the AuC possibly contributes to higher-order feedback processing of diverse auditory inputs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The tonotopic gradient is well preserved across all layers within the A1.
source: It is also known that the tonotopic gradient is well preserved across all layers within the A1 (Guo et al., 2012; Montes-Lourido et al., 2021; Tischbirek et al., 2019; Winkowski and Kanold, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: All previous discoveries in tonotopic mapping are based on layer specificity.
source: However, all of these previous discoveries in tonotopic mapping are based on layer specificity.
evidence: This is a characterization of previous research approaches.

claim: Neurons within the same layer can exhibit diversity in their molecular, morphological, physiological, and connectional features.
source: Neurons within the same layer can exhibit diversity in their molecular, morphological, physiological, and connectional features (Triarhou, 2021; Yarmohammadi et al., 2014), and therefore, categorizing cortical neurons based on their projection specificity can provide a deeper fundamental understanding of their functional organization.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Categorizing cortical neurons based on their projection specificity can provide a deeper fundamental understanding of their functional organization.
source: Neurons within the same layer can exhibit diversity in their molecular, morphological, physiological, and connectional features (Triarhou, 2021; Yarmohammadi et al., 2014), and therefore, categorizing cortical neurons based on their projection specificity can provide a deeper fundamental understanding of their functional organization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited knowledge about neuronal diversity.

claim: The A1-MGB projecting neurons play an essential role in the feedforward-feedback loop of the thalamus-neocortex interplay for integrated sound information processing flow.
source: The A1-MGB projecting neurons play an essential role in the feedforward-feedback loop of the thalamus-neocortex interplay for integrated sound information processing flow (Happel et al., 2010) and the perception of complex sounds (Clayton et al., 2021; Homma et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The A1-MGB projecting neurons play an essential role in the perception of complex sounds.
source: The A1-MGB projecting neurons play an essential role in the feedforward-feedback loop of the thalamus-neocortex interplay for integrated sound information processing flow (Happel et al., 2010) and the perception of complex sounds (Clayton et al., 2021; Homma et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There has been limited understanding of the functional properties of corticothalamic projecting neurons due to technical difficulties.
source: However, due to technical difficulties, there has been limited understanding of the functional properties of these specific corticothalamic projecting neurons (Antunes and Malmierca, 2021; Winer et al., 2001), because they are located in deeper layers of the cortex and are more difficult to access by means of commonly used, single-cell-resolving recording techniques such as conventional two-photon (2P) microscopy (Kobat et al., 2009; Oheim et al., 2001; Takasaki et al., 2020; Tischbirek et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Corticothalamic projecting neurons are located in deeper layers of the cortex and are more difficult to access by conventional two-photon (2P) microscopy.
source: However, due to technical difficulties, there has been limited understanding of the functional properties of these specific corticothalamic projecting neurons (Antunes and Malmierca, 2021; Winer et al., 2001), because they are located in deeper layers of the cortex and are more difficult to access by means of commonly used, single-cell-resolving recording techniques such as conventional two-photon (2P) microscopy (Kobat et al., 2009; Oheim et al., 2001; Takasaki et al., 2020; Tischbirek et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A rabies-based retrograde labeling method with pathway specificity has been established to circumvent the neuropil contamination problem associated with conventional 2P imaging for CT neurons.
source: Recent work has established a rabies-based retrograde labeling method with pathway specificity (Sun et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2020) to circumvent the neuropil contamination problem associated with conventional 2P imaging for CT neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TR neurons were labeled using an anterograde trans-synaptic tracing strategy by injecting a Cre-recombinase-expressing AAV into the MGB, then injecting a second AAV carrying Cre-dependent GCaMP6s in the AuC.
source: To label TR neurons, we used an anterograde trans-synaptic tracing strategy by injecting a Cre-recombinase-expressing AAV into the MGB, then injecting a second AAV carrying Cre-dependent GCaMP6s (AAV2/9-CaMKII-DIO-GCaMP6s) in the AuC (Figure 1A and B; Zingg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by data and citations.

claim: Neurons labeled with AAV-GCaMP6s were observed across all layers of the AuC.
source: Neurons labeled with AAV-GCaMP6s were observed across all layers of the AuC (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: CT neurons were labeled by performing retrograde tracing with a rabies virus CVS-N2c-derived vector (CVS-GCaMP6s) by injecting it into the MGB.
source: To label CT neurons, we performed retrograde tracing with a rabies virus CVS-N2c-derived vector (CVS-GCaMP6s) by injecting it into the MGB (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by data.

claim: Neurons labeled with CVS-GCaMP6s were restricted to AuC L6.
source: Neurons labeled with CVS-GCaMP6s were restricted to AuC L6 (Figure 1F and G) and were then imaged by 2P Ca2+ imaging, in line with our recent work (Gu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures and citations.

claim: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings and in vivo 2P imaging showed no change in electrophysiological, morphological, or functional characteristics of CVS-labeled CT neurons.
source: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings and in vivo 2P imaging showed no change in electrophysiological, morphological, or functional characteristics of CVS-labeled CT neurons (Gu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The low-frequency (LF) tone (4 kHz) elicited spatially restricted responses in the regions referred to as 'LF area'.
source: To locate A1, we conducted wide-field imaging in awake GCaMP6s-labeled mice and defined that the low-frequency (LF) tone (4 kHz) elicited spatially restricted responses in the regions referred to as 'LF area', and that the high-frequency (HF) tone (32 kHz) elicited responses in the regions referred to as 'HF area' (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The high-frequency (HF) tone (32 kHz) elicited responses in the regions referred to as 'HF area'.
source: To locate A1, we conducted wide-field imaging in awake GCaMP6s-labeled mice and defined that the low-frequency (LF) tone (4 kHz) elicited spatially restricted responses in the regions referred to as 'LF area', and that the high-frequency (HF) tone (32 kHz) elicited responses in the regions referred to as 'HF area' (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: In AAV-GCaMP6s labeled mice, the locations of A1, anterior auditory field (AAF), and secondary auditory field (A2) were identified based on the known tonotopy in mice.
source: In AAV-GCaMP6s labeled mice, we identified the locations of A1, anterior auditory field (AAF), and secondary auditory field (A2) based on the known tonotopy in mice (Figure 1H, left panel) (Issa et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: In CVS-GCaMP6s-labeled (i.e. CT neurons) mice, pure tone stimulation elicited wide-field signals in only one auditory region that exhibited a tonotopic gradient.
source: It is worth noting that, in CVS-GCaMP6s-labeled (i.e. CT neurons) mice, pure tone stimulation elicited wide-field signals in only one auditory region that exhibited a tonotopic gradient (Figure 1H, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Injection of CTB-555 into the CVS-GCaMP6s-labeled region resulted in clearly visible CTB-555-labeled cell bodies in the MGBv, suggesting that CVS-GCaMP6s-labeled neurons were located in A1.
source: To identify this region in AuC, we injected a retrograde tracing indicator cholera toxin subunit B conjugated with Alexa 555 (CTB-555) into this region, which resulted in clearly visible CTB-555-labeled cell bodies in the MGBv (Figure 1I), suggesting that CVS-GCaMP6s-labeled neurons were located in A1 (Rothschild et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: The average power delivered to the brain during 2P imaging was in the range of 30—120 mW, depending on the depth of imaging.
source: When performing 2P imaging, the average power delivered to the brain was in the range of 30—120 mW, depending on the depth of imaging.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the study.

claim: At 7 and 13 days after CVS injection, CVS-labeled neurons had completely normal response properties.
source: At 7 and 13 days after injection, we found that CVS-labeled neurons had completely normal response properties (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: High-titer AAV1-Cre virus has been reported to anterogradely label postsynaptic neurons and also retrogradely label presynaptic neurons.
source: High-titer AAV1-Cre virus has been reported to anterogradely label postsynaptic neurons and also retrogradely label presynaptic neurons (Zingg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: To minimize labeling ambiguity, 2P imaging depth of TR neurons was restricted to 200—400 μm, without imaging the neurons in L5 and L6.
source: To minimize this labeling ambiguity, we restricted the 2P imaging depth of TR neurons to 200—400 μm, without imaging the neurons in L5 and L6, which were reciprocally connected with the MGB (Harris and Mrsic-Flogel, 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological decision supported by citation.

claim: L5 and L6 neurons are reciprocally connected with the MGB.
source: To minimize this labeling ambiguity, we restricted the 2P imaging depth of TR neurons to 200—400 μm, without imaging the neurons in L5 and L6, which were reciprocally connected with the MGB (Harris and Mrsic-Flogel, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A total of 1041 TR neurons were imaged in 5 animals.
source: In total, we imaged 1041 TR neurons in 5 animals.
evidence: This is a data summary from the study.

claim: 46% of TR neurons were 'tuned' neurons, 41% were 'irregular' neurons, and 13% were 'silent' neurons.
source: 46% were 'tuned' neurons, 41% were 'irregular' neurons, and 13% were 'silent' neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, the definitions of 'irregular', 'tuned', and 'silent', see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: A total of 2721 CT neurons were imaged from 10 animals.
source: For CT neurons, we imaged a total of 2721 neurons from 10 animals.
evidence: This is a data summary from the study.

claim: 18% of CT neurons were 'tuned' neurons, 57% were 'irregular' neurons, and 25% were 'silent' neurons.
source: 18% were 'tuned' neurons, 57% were 'irregular' neurons, and 25% were 'silent' neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: For TR neurons, a clear tonotopic axis was observed in the organization of median BF (R=0.77, p<0.001; 2.13 octaves/mm).
source: For TR neurons, we observed a clear tonotopic axis in the organization of median BF (R=0.77, p<0.001; 2.13 octaves/mm; Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in the figures.

claim: No tonotopic gradient was observed in CT neurons (R=0.20, p=0.21; 0.21 octaves/mm).
source: However, no such tonotopic gradient was observed in CT neurons (R=0.20, p=0.21; 0.21 octaves/mm; Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Plotting the relative positions of all individual tuned TR neurons revealed a significant low-to-high frequency gradient from caudal to rostral (R=0.52, p<0.001; 1.76 octaves/mm).
source: Plotting the relative positions of all individual tuned TR or CT neurons in each mouse revealed a significant low-to-high frequency gradient from caudal to rostral for TR neurons (R=0.52, p<0.001; 1.76 octaves/mm; Figure 2I and J), but an absence of tonotopy in CT neurons (R=0.079, p=0.084; 0.37 octaves/mm; Figure 2K and L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in the figures.

claim: There was an absence of tonotopy in CT neurons (R=0.079, p=0.084; 0.37 octaves/mm).
source: Plotting the relative positions of all individual tuned TR or CT neurons in each mouse revealed a significant low-to-high frequency gradient from caudal to rostral for TR neurons (R=0.52, p<0.001; 1.76 octaves/mm; Figure 2I and J), but an absence of tonotopy in CT neurons (R=0.079, p=0.084; 0.37 octaves/mm; Figure 2K and L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The results at single-neuron resolution confirmed that the TR neuronal population does possess tonotopy, as previous reports have shown on a coarse scale.
source: These results, at single-neuron resolution, confirmed that the TR neuronal population does possess tonotopy, as previous reports have shown on a coarse scale (Kalatsky et al., 2005; Wu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data supported by citations.

claim: Both TR and CT neurons displayed no obvious pattern of BF distribution throughout A1.
source: The fraction of different BF-responsive neurons among TR and CT neurons showed that both TR and CT neurons displayed no obvious pattern throughout A1 (Figure 2M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Higher proportions of TR neurons responded to LF sounds in the LF areas or HF sounds in the HF areas.
source: When categorized into LF or HF areas, higher proportions of TR neurons responded to LF sounds in the LF areas or HF sounds in the HF areas, whereas CT neurons showed no frequency preference in either area (Figure 2N and O).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: CT neurons showed no frequency preference in either LF or HF areas.
source: When categorized into LF or HF areas, higher proportions of TR neurons responded to LF sounds in the LF areas or HF sounds in the HF areas, whereas CT neurons showed no frequency preference in either area (Figure 2N and O).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The discrepancy between 2P imaging showing no tonotopic gradient of L6 CT neurons and wide-field epifluorescence imaging showing a tonotopic gradient could be largely due to differences in the imaging methods.
source: Note the obvious discrepancy in that the 2P imaging data here shows no tonotopic gradient of L6 CT neurons, but wide-field epifluorescence imaging data shows the presence of a tonotopic gradient from the same mice (Figure 1H), which could be largely due to differences in the imaging methods and will be discussed later on.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observed differences.

claim: Control experiments imaging general excitatory neurons in superficial layers showed a clear tonotopic gradient, consistent with previous findings.
source: To validate the reliability of our imaging/analysis approach, we performed control experiments that imaged the general excitatory neurons in superficial layers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and the results showed a clear tonotopic gradient, which was consistent with previous findings (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2010; Romero et al., 2020; Rothschild et al., 2010; Tischbirek et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: No significant differences were found in the fraction of tuned neurons, field interquartile range (IQR), or BWmax between TR neurons in L2/3 versus those in L4.
source: We found no significant differences in the fraction of tuned neurons, field interquartile range (IQR), or BWmax between TR neurons in L2/3 versus those in L4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: TR neurons are significantly more likely to be tuned to pure tones than their neighboring non-TR excitatory neurons.
source: Our results show that TR neurons are significantly more likely to be tuned to pure tones than their neighboring non-TR excitatory neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: A neuron's long-range connectivity, and not just its laminar location, is a key determinant of its response properties.
source: This finding provides direct evidence that a neuron's long-range connectivity, and not just its laminar location, is a key determinant of its response properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: TR neurons exhibited similar frequency preference in HF or LF areas.
source: Examination of BF distribution among TR or CT neurons revealed that TR neurons exhibited similar frequency preference in HF or LF areas (Figure 3A), whereas CT neurons displayed high heterogeneity in their frequency preferences, regardless of LF or HF areas (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: CT neurons displayed high heterogeneity in their frequency preferences, regardless of LF or HF areas.
source: Examination of BF distribution among TR or CT neurons revealed that TR neurons exhibited similar frequency preference in HF or LF areas (Figure 3A), whereas CT neurons displayed high heterogeneity in their frequency preferences, regardless of LF or HF areas (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: CT neurons had higher IQRBF than TR neurons across all focal planes.
source: Quantitative analysis showed that CT neurons had higher IQRBF than TR neurons across all focal planes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: CT neurons had significantly higher IQRBF than TR neurons in LF areas but showed no significant difference from TR neurons in HF areas at the focal plane level.
source: Similarly, evaluation of LF or HF areas indicated that CT neurons had significantly higher IQRBF than TR neurons in LF areas but showed no significant difference from TR neurons in HF areas at the focal plane level (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: TR neurons exhibited lower median IQRBF than CT neurons at the local scale.
source: The results revealed that TR neurons also exhibited lower median IQRBF than CT neurons at the local scale (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: CT neurons had significantly higher local IQRBF than TR neurons in LF areas.
source: Consistent with the focal plane scale, CT neurons had significantly higher local IQRBF than TR neurons in LF areas (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The local IQRBF of TR neurons in HF areas was significantly higher than that of TR neurons in LF areas.
source: Unexpectedly, the local IQRBF of TR neurons in HF areas was significantly higher than that of TR neurons in LF areas (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The local IQRBF of TR neurons followed a low-to-high gradient along the caudal-to-rostral axis (R=0.2655, p=0.0032).
source: Further analysis across local regions revealed that the local IQRBF of TR neurons followed a low-to-high gradient along the caudal-to-rostral axis (R=0.2655, p=0.0032; Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Δfrequency between nearest-neighboring TR or CT neurons was consistent with results of local IQRBF analysis.
source: The analysis of Δfrequency (BF variability) (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2010; Zeng et al., 2019) between nearest-neighboring TR or CT neurons was consistent with results of local IQRBF analysis (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: Δfrequency followed a clear gradient in the organization of TR neurons along the caudal-to-rostral axis (R=0.2463, p<0.001).
source: That is, Δfrequency followed a clear gradient in the organization of TR neurons along the caudal-to-rostral axis (R=0.2463, p<0.001; Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in the figures.

claim: TR neurons, but not CT neurons, displayed high IQRBF in HF areas compared to LF areas.
source: Moreover, TR neurons, but not CT neurons, displayed high IQRBF in HF areas compared to LF areas (Figure 3G and I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: A higher proportion of CT neurons was associated with V-shaped FRAs than TR neurons.
source: We found that a higher proportion of CT neurons was associated with V-shaped FRAs than TR neurons, whereas the proportion of CT neurons associated with I-shaped FRAs was lower than that of TR neurons (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The proportion of CT neurons associated with I-shaped FRAs was lower than that of TR neurons.
source: We found that a higher proportion of CT neurons was associated with V-shaped FRAs than TR neurons, whereas the proportion of CT neurons associated with I-shaped FRAs was lower than that of TR neurons (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: No difference was detected in the proportions of CT and TR neurons associated with O-shaped FRAs.
source: By contrast, no difference was detected in the proportions of CT and TR neurons associated with O-shaped FRAs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The half-peak bandwidth of CT neurons was significantly wider than that of TR neurons.
source: This analysis showed that the half-peak bandwidth of CT neurons was significantly wider than that of TR neurons (Figure 4D), while the Q value of CT neurons was lower than that of TR neurons, especially in the HF areas (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The Q value of CT neurons was lower than that of TR neurons, especially in the HF areas.

claim: Higher Q values indicate sharper tuning of neurons, which suggests higher frequency discrimination.
source: Since higher Q values indicate sharper tuning of neurons, which suggests higher frequency discrimination (Micheyl et al., 2013), these results suggest that TR neurons might be responsible for finer tone discrimination.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TR neurons might be responsible for finer tone discrimination.
source: Since higher Q values indicate sharper tuning of neurons, which suggests higher frequency discrimination (Micheyl et al., 2013), these results suggest that TR neurons might be responsible for finer tone discrimination.

claim: The BWmax of TR neurons was significantly narrower than that of CT neurons, irrespective of the FRA shape.

claim: The distribution of TR neurons generally peaked at a BWmax of 1—2 octaves, while the distribution of CT neurons peaked at a BWmax of 3—4 octaves.

claim: CT neurons had significantly higher BWmax than TR neurons.

claim: TR neurons had a significantly narrower BWmax range than CT neurons in either LF or HF areas.
source: Within LF or HF areas, TR neurons had a significantly narrower BWmax range than CT neurons in either area.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: TR neurons in HF areas had a significantly lower BWmax than TR neurons in LF areas.
source: Surprisingly, TR neurons in HF areas had a significantly lower BWmax than TR neurons in LF areas (Figure 4J), suggesting that the BWmax distribution among TR neurons might change along the caudal-to-rostral axis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The BWmax distribution among TR neurons might change along the caudal-to-rostral axis.

claim: The MI distribution across both TR and CT neuronal populations peaked at 1.

claim: The fraction of neurons exhibiting non-monotonic intensity response did not significantly differ between TR and CT neurons.
source: Subsequent categorization as either monotonic or non-monotonic (using a criterion of MI = 0.5 [de la Rocha et al., 2008; Moore and Wehr, 2013], neurons with an index <0.5 considered intensity-tuned) showed that the fraction of neurons exhibiting non-monotonic intensity response did not significantly differ between TR and CT neurons (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: A higher proportion of non-monotonic CT neurons than TR were located in LF areas.
source: However, examination of MI values within LF or HF areas showed that a higher proportion of non-monotonic CT neurons than TR were located in LF areas, while a larger proportion of non-monotonic TR neurons was located in HF areas than in LF areas (Figure 4M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: A larger proportion of non-monotonic TR neurons was located in HF areas than in LF areas.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Among non-monotonic neurons, TR neurons had higher MI than CT neurons.
source: In addition, among non-monotonic neurons, TR neurons had higher MI than CT neurons, whereas monotonic TR neurons had a lower MI than monotonic CT neurons (Figure 4N).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Monotonic TR neurons had a lower MI than monotonic CT neurons.
source: In addition, among non-monotonic neurons, TR neurons had higher MI than CT neurons, whereas monotonic TR neurons had a lower MI than monotonic CT neurons (Figure 4N).

claim: Non-monotonic CT neurons had a higher BF than monotonic CT neurons.
source: Furthermore, we note that non-monotonic CT neurons had a higher BF than monotonic CT neurons, whereas the BF was similar between monotonic and non-monotonic TR neurons (Figure 4O).

claim: BWmax did not significantly differ between monotonic and non-monotonic neurons in either the TR or CT populations.

claim: BWmax, which reflects the degree of integration of synaptic inputs from presynaptic neurons, is 3.0 octaves in CT neurons, but only 1.3 octaves in TR neurons, indicative of an increase in synaptic integration during cortical processing.
source: For example, BWmax, which reflects the degree of integration of synaptic inputs from presynaptic neurons (Kratz and Manis, 2015; Li et al., 2019; Schreiner and Sutter, 1992), is 3.0 octaves in CT neurons, but only 1.3 octaves in TR neurons (Figure 4I), indicative of an increase in synaptic integration during cortical processing (Li et al., 2019).

claim: The lack of tonotopy is an active computation, not a passive degradation.

source: Instead of relaying 'what' frequency was heard, the descending signal from CT neurons may convey more abstract, higher-order information – such as the behavioral relevance of a sound, predictions about upcoming sounds, or motor-related efference copy signals – that are not inherently frequency-specific (Wang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022).

claim: The descending A1-to-MGB pathway is often considered to be modulatory, shaping thalamic responses rather than driving them directly.
source: The descending A1-to-MGB pathway is often considered to be modulatory, shaping thalamic responses rather than driving them directly.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the pathway.

claim: A modulatory signal designed to globally adjust thalamic gain or selectivity may not require, and may even be hindered by, a fine-grained topographical organization.
source: A modulatory signal designed to globally adjust thalamic gain or selectivity may not require, and may even be hindered by, a fine-grained topographical organization.

claim: The sensory information flow descending from the A1 to the thalamus via L6 CT neurons does not arrange tonotopically.
source: In summary, our findings fill in a knowledge gap in the auditory physiology: whereas the corticothalamic feedback projection is known to contribute to higher cognitive processing of behaviorally relevant complex sounds, the basic pure tone map that underlies and facilitates this advanced processing remained unclear. Our results reveal that the sensory information flow descending from the A1 to the thalamus via L6 CT neurons does not arrange tonotopically.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Categorizing cortical neurons based on their projection specificity represents an advance in the conceptual framework for functional organization.
source: The new shift, categorizing cortical neurons based on their projection specificity, represents an advance in the conceptual framework for functional organization.
